name: David Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the office administrator at a haulage depot, forty lorries and about fifty drivers, on the ring road outside a port town. I sort the drivers' hours paperwork, book delivery slots at the warehouses, chase missing delivery notes and do the holiday rota. It's a portacabin with two transport planners and me, and the radio's always on.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the drivers, they're funny and they treat the office like a café. What wears me out is chasing paperwork, because a missing delivery note means the customer won't pay, and somehow that's my fault. Pay's on the low side, and my girlfriend Priya's a nurse on shifts, so we're fine month to month but there's maybe two weeks of money in the account at any time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. I'll read it out. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was a bit of a damp squib and move on. Our planners would be glad, they were nervous about route-planning software. I'd probably share a meme about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a bit of relief. Some of my paperwork would get quicker, like matching delivery notes to invoices, and I'd use whatever tool does that. The bigger thing for me is that haulage is up and down. In haulage, when a big contract goes, the office gets cut before the drivers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job and use the AI tool for the boring matching work if the firm gets one. I'd try to save a bit more, maybe a hundred a month, because two weeks is nothing. And I'd keep an eye on who the firm's contracts are with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, the normal amount. It's the money more than the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened the last time a contract went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years ago we lost a supermarket contract, and they let go of one of the two office staff. It wasn't me, but it was close. Since then I've done both jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Priya's job make you feel safer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, a lot. Nurses don't get laid off in this town, they're always short. But her pay alone doesn't cover the rent and the car, so we'd still be scraping by.

say: I'd call it a **damp squib** and move on.
I'd say the planners would be glad about the **route software** staying away.
think: Some **paperwork matching** gets quicker, and I'd use the tool for it.
Haulage is **up and down**, and the office is cut before the drivers.
do: Use any AI tool for **delivery-note matching**.
S0.quote: In haulage, when a big contract goes, the office gets cut before the drivers.
fieldNote: David's worry is the **contract cycle**, which already cost one office job.
His partner's **nursing job** steadies the household but doesn't cover the rent alone.
He is open to AI for **boring matching** work once it's proven.

steps.text: Use the firm's AI tool to match delivery notes to invoices
Save a hundred a month towards a cushion
Keep doing the drivers' paperwork and holiday rota as usual

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. I'll read it out. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming, so firms should bring people along with it, not just switch them off. I'd say that at work. Some changes are good, but not if they cost the people who keep things running.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think most of my job goes into software over a few years. Booking slots, chasing notes, checking hours, all that is exactly what the card says. The drivers are safe for a while because robots are slower, but the office shrinks to one planner who runs the system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the depot manager to put me on the training for the new system as soon as it's mentioned. I'd learn the planning side from Kev (the senior transport planner), because a planner is more likely to stay than an admin. And I'd cut back on the car payments by selling the car and getting something cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's real, but I think I can do something about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Kev teach you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, he's always said he wants to retire in a few years. If I can do his job by then, the firm has a reason to keep me. I'd rather be the planner than the paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Priya?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her it's not a disaster yet but I need to move up or move out. She'd say go for it. She always does.

say: I'd say firms should **bring people along**, not switch them off.
I'd say change is fine, but not at the cost of **the people** keeping things running.
think: Booking slots, **chasing notes** and checking hours go to software.
The office shrinks to **one planner** running the system.
do: Ask to join the **training** for the new system.
Swap the car for a **cheaper one**.
feel: **Anxious**, but I feel I can do something.
S1.quote: I'd rather be the planner than the paperwork.
fieldNote: David reads the card as **his job list** and plans to move up to planner.
He relies on Kev, a **retiring planner**, as his route in.
Cutting the **car payments** is his first money move.

steps.text: Ask the depot manager for a place on the new system training
Learn transport planning from the senior planner before he retires
Sell the car and buy a cheaper one

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. I'll read it out. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for anyone, and governments need to put something in place, like money while people retrain. I'm not a big politics person, but I'd vote for whoever had a real plan. At work I'd say let's not panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm out of office work by 2028, and so is Kev, because AGI plans routes better than he does. The drivers last until about 2031 when the robots come, then the lorries drive themselves. So the whole depot goes, just in two waves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at getting my lorry licence straight away, because it buys me about three years of driving work. The firm sometimes pays for it if you sign on for two years. Priya and I would cut spending to the essentials and put off moving to a bigger place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Driving buys three years. Then what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know. I'd hope by then there's something new, like people looking after the robots, or the government's sorted something. Three years of a driver's wage is better than nothing while I work it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Priya's job change how you feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the one thing that stops me panicking. Hospitals will still need nurses for a long time, even with robots. We'd be poorer, but we'd eat.

say: I'd say it's **too fast**, and government should pay people to retrain.
I'd vote for whoever had a **real plan**.
think: I'm out of **office work** by 2028, and so is the planner.
The depot goes in **two waves**: office first, then drivers around 2031.
do: Get my **lorry licence** straight away, ideally firm-funded.
Put off moving to a **bigger place**.
S2.quote: Hospitals will still need nurses for a long time, even with robots. We'd be poorer, but we'd eat.
fieldNote: David sees the depot going in **two waves**, office first and drivers later.
He uses the **three-year gap** by getting a lorry licence.
His partner's **nursing job** is the one thing between him and panic.

steps.text: Get a lorry licence through the firm's two-year deal
Cut spending to rent, food and bills
Put off moving to a bigger flat with Priya
Vote for the party with a real retraining plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. I'll read it out. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if people start now. Firms should tell staff early what they're planning. I'd say that to the depot manager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to become a planner first and maybe get the licence too. My office work still goes by 2031, but I'd have the driving to fall back on until about 2034. It's not safe, but it's a few steps instead of a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn planning from Kev in the first year and take over some of his routes. I'd get the lorry licence in year two as a backup. And I'd save hard, maybe a month's money by the end of year two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd sleep most nights. It's more of a staircase than a drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why both planning and a licence?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't know which one lasts longer. Planning is thinking work, so AGI gets it in 2031. Driving is hands-on, so robots get it around 2034. Having both means I'm not stuck on one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut to save that month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Takeaways and the football subscription. Maybe the holiday to Priya's sister. Those add up to a couple of hundred a month.

fieldNote: David reasons clearly about **thinking versus hands-on** timing for his two options.
He spreads risk with **two skills** rather than betting on one.

steps.text: Take over some of the senior planner's routes in year one
Save one month of expenses by the end of year two
Drop takeaways and the football subscription

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. I'll read it out. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, so we should use it sensibly. I'd tell people to learn the new stuff as it comes. And I'd say governments have no excuse not to plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years, I'd be thirty-seven. I could train in something completely different, maybe the maintenance side of the depot, or electrical work. I still think my office job goes, but I'd have time to find something that lasts longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look into an electrician course at the college, part-time over three or four years. I'd keep working at the depot meanwhile and use the AI tools as they come in. And Priya and I would probably think about buying a small place once she gets her next pay grade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, but quieter. It's in the back of my mind rather than the front.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why electrical work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle's an electrician and he's never short of work. And someone's going to have to wire up all these robots and chargers. It's hands-on, so robots come late to it, and even then it's complicated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you actually buy a house with all this coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. It feels a bit mad, but Priya's job is solid, and renting forever isn't great either. We'd buy something small and cheap, not stretch ourselves.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the whole depot goes in two waves and I've got two weeks of money. What would help is the firm paying for licences and courses before the cuts, not after, and some money from the government while you retrain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the drivers. Everyone thinks about the lorries driving themselves, but nobody asks who'll check them. A depot without people would be a strange, quiet place.

headlineQuote: A depot without people would be a strange, quiet place.
portrait: David is **27**, office administrator at a haulage depot near a port town, living with Priya, a nurse.
He has about **two weeks** of money, and his partner's steady job is the household's anchor.
He's **centre-minded** and practical, open to AI once it's proven.
He plans in steps: **planner**, then a lorry licence, then perhaps electrical work.
He reasons about **thinking versus hands-on** timing for each option.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the depot goes in two waves and he has little money.
whatWouldHelp: Firms paying for **licences and courses** before the cuts.
